# I0338-M3 Dossier: Cattle Lien Registry and Sale-Barn Exit Alerts

Research date: 2026-10-13. Items marked (S) were read only in a search-result summary, not a fetched page. Every figure below has a source or is labeled an assumption.

## 1. Verdict

Provisional: **weakened, not dead.** The 30-day manual pilot is cheap and still worth running, but four load-bearing premises of the pitch did not survive checking:

1. The headline fraud case is a different fraud type from the one the product catches.
2. Federal law gives sale barns more protection than the pitch assumes, which weakens "barns pay twice, so they will fund this."
3. Sale-barn software and state brand agencies already offer lien checks and lender-facing registries.
4. Public price anchors are 6-12x below the proposed $300-600 per loan per year.

My bottom-up estimate puts the Phase 1 pool near $4-13M a year at 100% penetration (Section 3). That is a niche business unless the Phase 3 registry is both built and adopted.

## 2. Pitch claims versus verified facts

| Pitch claim | Finding |
|---|---|
| Parent fraud case: "$2.8M loan against 850 head" shows double-pledging | The case is Craig Johnson, a Missouri bank vice president and pastor, who pleaded guilty to at least $9.3M of fraud. Prosecutors say he never bought cattle, and the "850 cow-calf pairs for $2.8M" was a forged bill of sale. The article mentions no liens and no sale barns. [KCTV5, 2026-09-10](https://www.kctv5.com/2026/09/10/former-bank-vp-pastor-pleads-guilty-multi-million-dollar-cattle-investment-fraud-scheme/) |
| Markets "end up paying twice" on conversion | Partly true under old common law; the Food Security Act (FSA) largely displaced it. See Section 4. |
| State agencies are passive, paper or annual lists | Contradicted for Montana (live brand-lien portal) and Alberta (paid alert service). See Section 5. |
| EID tags are more common after the Nov 2024 rule | The rule took effect 2024-11-05 but covers sexually intact cattle and bison 18 months or older, dairy cattle and rodeo/exhibition cattle, and grandfathers previously tagged animals. Steers and feeder calves are not covered. Brands and tattoos are unchanged. [Federal Register](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-05-09/html/2024-09717.htm), [PCFB summary](https://pcfb.org/usda-announces-aphis-final-rule-on-electronic-id-in-cattle/). I did not check for later changes. |
| Record prices raise dollars at risk | Prices peaked in May 2026 (five-area steer $2.63/lb) and have fallen since. [FoodMarket](https://www.foodmarket.com/News/A/1349621/ANALYSIS-US-2026-Live-Cattle-Rally-Loses-Steam-Steer-Prices-Fall-Nearly-10-percent-from-Record-Highs) (S). Oklahoma 500-548 lb steers averaged $408/cwt in the week ending Sept 5, versus about $516 in late April. [USDA AMS Sept 2026](https://s3.amazonaws.com/barchart-news-store-prod/external_links/USDA/20260904-AMS_1831.pdf), [USDA AMS Apr 2026](https://mymarketnews.ams.usda.gov/filerepo/sites/default/files/1831/2026-04-19/1319944/ams_1831_00352.pdf) (S) |

## 3. Market context and bottom-up sizing

**Cattle base.** The US herd was 86.2M head on Jan 1, 2026, a 75-year low, with 27.6M beef cows and 4.71M beef replacement heifers (+1%). [DTN](https://www.dtnpf.com/agriculture/web/ag/news/article/2026/01/30/jan-1-cattle-inventory-slightly-year)

**Lender universe.** At Q4 2025, 3,334 commercial banks held farm loans, of which 933 met the 25%-of-loans "agricultural bank" test. Farm loans at banks totaled $207.4B ($119.8B real estate, $87.6B production). [farmdoc daily, Apr 2026](https://farmdocdaily.illinois.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/fdd040226.pdf) (S). Farm Credit System associations are additional lenders; I did not verify their count.

**Auction base.** About 32M cattle a year sell through auctions (2020 P&S data); the Livestock Marketing Association (LMA) says it represents 85% of markets. [LMA](https://www.lmaweb.com/NewsAndMedia/PressReleases/economic-impact-study-lma-2023) The pitch's "10M+ head" is conservative. I found no current national market count. A research list shows 1,619 known cattle markets for 2012-2016, including closed ones. [Dryad](https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.cfxpnvxg7) South Dakota listed 27 licensed markets in 2020. [SD AIB](https://aib.sd.gov/auctionmkts.html) Barns are closing as herds shrink. [FERN](https://thefern.org/ag_insider/as-cattle-numbers-drop-livestock-auction-barns-close)

**Exit coverage.** Auction barns handled about 69% of reported feeder and stocker receipts; direct sales ran about 16% and video/internet about 15%. The shares sum above 100%, so treat them as approximate. [Farm Bureau/USDA-AMS](https://www.fb.org/market-intel/marketing-feeder-cattle-changes-in-sales-data) (S). Fed cattle going feedyard to packer also bypass barns. "Watch the gates" therefore covers a majority of feeder exits, not all.

**Phase 1 pool (assumptions marked A).**
- 933 ag banks x 30% with material cattle books (A) = about 280 banks.
- 150 monitored loans per bank (the pitch's figure, unverified) = about 42,000 loans.
- At $100 / $300 / $600 per loan per year: **$4.2M / $12.6M / $25M** at 100% penetration. The $100 case is about 2x the Alberta price anchor in Section 7.
- Phase 3 per-head fee: 32M head x $0.10-0.25 = $3.2-8M at 100% capture.
- Combined realistic pool: about $7-21M a year. Five-year penetration of 20-30% implies roughly $1.5-6M ARR. Registry lookups and advance-fee share are unsized.

## 4. Legal and liability landscape

**The FSA sharply limits market exposure.** Under 7 U.S.C. §1631(g), a commission merchant or selling agent generally is *not* subject to the seller's security interest, even if perfected and known. Exceptions: (A) written notice within one year before the sale, with prescribed content (lender and debtor names and addresses, a tax identifier, product description, county); (C) in a central-filing state, the agent failed to register with the Secretary of State and the lender filed an effective financing statement (EFS); or (D) the agent received written notice from the Secretary of State and did not obtain a waiver or release. [Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/7/1631)

Implications:
- Barns are exposed only after notice or non-registration, so they have a reason to avoid formal notice, not to welcome it. Pre-1985 cases holding auctioneers liable even without knowledge ([Commercial Bank at Alma v. Hales](https://cite.case.law/ark/281/439/) (S)) predate the FSA.
- A product that delivers lender profiles to barns may turn them into noticed parties. Whether a platform feed meets the notice-content rules is a question for counsel.
- Fuzzy matching addresses a documented failure. In *Fin-Ag v. Pipestone*, 2008 SD 48, the lender's EFS omitted the seller's d.b.a. (C&M Dairy). The case reached a cert petition (No. 08-576), where the Solicitor General recommended denial. [SG brief](https://www.justice.gov/osg/brief/fin-ag-inc-v-pipestone-livestock-auction-mkt-inc-amicus-invitation-petition), [SD opinion](https://ujs.sd.gov/media/1vdfl5cp/23982.pdf) (S). Lenders can fix this by listing all names on the EFS, which makes the product a convenience layer on an existing legal tool.

**Central filing.** USDA says 19 states have certified systems; I confirmed 12 (AL, CO, ID, LA, ME, MN, MS, MT, NE, NH, NM, ND), and the other seven were cut off. [USDA AMS](https://www.ams.usda.gov/node/29815) (S; the page returned 403 on fetch). In Nebraska, buyers and commission merchants register annually with the Secretary of State to receive the master lists. [Neb. LB1035](https://www.NebraskaLegislature.gov/FloorDocs/104/PDF/Slip/LB1035.pdf) (S) North Dakota sells an agricultural lien buyer's report for $480 a year. [ND SOS](https://sos.nd.gov/node/4643) (S)

**Packers and Stockyards.** Sale proceeds run through custodial accounts. Montana, for example, exempts licensed markets only if proceeds go through such an account. [Montana Livestock Sale Application](https://prod-liv.mt.gov/_docs/BE/Forms/Livestock-Sale-Application_11-2024.pdf) (S)

**Not researched:** Gramm-Leach-Bliley limits on lenders uploading borrower names to a third party; state data law; and whether alerts could create negligence claims if a missed alert precedes a loss.

## 5. Competitors and incumbents

|---|---|---|---|

Washington State Dept. of Agriculture is co-developing a module so brand inspectors verify ownership inside Sale Time. [WSDA](https://agr.wa.gov/departments/animals-livestock-and-pets/livestock/sale-time-at-the-auction). Customer count and pricing are not public. |
| ViewTrak (TrustBIX, TSXV: TBIX) | Auction Master Pro and Market Master | Adjacent; no lien module described | Claims 400+ locations as of a Nov 2021 release. [Newsfile](https://www.newsfilecorp.com/release/102929/TrustBIX-Subsidiary-ViewTrak-Technologies-Commercializes-Three-New-Modules-for-Auction-Software) |
| Montana Dept. of Livestock Brand Lien Portal | Lenders file a Notice of Security Interest against a recorded brand; $25 per transaction, no annual or search fee | **Direct in brand states.** It covers only animals bearing the borrower's brand. The page documents no alert feature. | [MDOL](https://liv.mt.gov/brands-enforcement/Brands-Liens), [portal](https://app.mt.gov/brandliens/Help/Instructions) |

Lender-requested inspections are chargeable. | Partial | [Neb. §54-1,100](https://nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/statutes.php?statute=54-1,100), [LB646 amendment](https://www.nebraskalegislature.gov/FloorDocs/109/PDF/AM/AM1342.pdf) (S) |

No lender product found. | Adjacent; plausible white-label partner | [MarketBeat](https://www.marketbeat.com/instant-alerts/where-food-comes-from-q4-earnings-call-highlights-2026-02-27/) (S) |

The grant's claim that about 75% of US cattle are bought with bank loans is unverified. |
| Cattler (Lincoln, NE) | Feedlot and ranch management software, "hundreds" of customers | Adjacent. Its page mentions no lender or lien features, though one search summary said otherwise. | [Cattler](https://cattler.farm/services-4) |
| Abroad: Cowmed/B3 (Brazil); E-Livestock (Zimbabwe) | Collar or RFID data tied to credit instruments | Phase 3 analogs, built with exchange or bank partners | [CryptoSlate](https://cryptoslate.com/how-10-cows-in-brazil-unlocked-a-path-to-bridge-an-8-trillion-global-finance-gap/) (S) |

**No US startup found** selling cross-barn consignment alerts to lenders. That reflects thin search coverage, not proof of absence. The finalist file's prior check ran no searches.

**Who could add this:** Sale Time (lien and brand modules already shipped) and state brand agencies (Montana, Alberta precedent). Their neutrality gap is real, but a barn-software vendor can offer a free lien-matching feed to its own customer base.

## 6. Evidence of demand and willingness to pay

**Real losses exist, but mostly by other mechanisms.**
- Rabo Agrifinance alleges about $50.6M unpaid on McClain feedyards. Reported inventory fell from 89,522 to 37,992 head by February, and nearly 78,000 head may have been sold or moved. Rabo's audit began only after missed April payments. [DTN](https://www.dtnpf.com/agriculture/web/ag/livestock/article/2023/05/10/rabo-asks-bankruptcy-court-subpoenas) The article does not name auction markets. This is the best "monitor the exits" case, but it is feedyard-scale, and a missed-payment trigger came before any barn alert would have.
- Texas: $5.8M against 8,000 head pledged, none found, with other people's cattle shown to the bank. [Ag Proud](https://agproud.com/articles/51727-texas-man-arrested-for-5-8-million-fraud-involving-8-000-cattle) A 2026 Decatur case involves a $5.5M loan on 3,000+ head and a refused inspection. [HPJ](https://hpj.com/2026/06/19/texas-man-arrested-in-cattle-collateral-case/) (S)
- Montana's Mack sold cattle securing loans from two lenders and kept the proceeds. [DOJ](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mt/pr/lewistown-man-sentenced-bank-fraud-obtaining-loans-cattle-ranching-business) An Arkansas woman is charged with keeping sale proceeds on a $214K estate loan (allegation). [SW Arkansas Radio](https://southwestarkansasradio.com/ashdown-woman-charged-in-alleged-cattle-sale-loan-fraud-case/)
- Eastern Livestock (2010) was check-kiting against sellers, with $81-130M of bad checks and 743 producers hit. [Farm and Dairy](https://www.farmanddairy.com/?p=18908) (S) It is a buyer-side payment-risk story, not a lien-exit story.

**Pattern:** the cases I found are mostly phantom collateral, inspection evasion or insider fraud. Only the Mack and Arkansas cases fit "pledged cattle sold, proceeds kept," and both are small. I found no dataset on lender losses by mechanism, no RFP, and no forum thread asking for a consignment alert.

**Spend on workarounds:** inspection mandates exist but target counts. Nebraska's livestock-loan rule calls for inspection within 30 days of origination, yearly follow-ups and head counts. [Neb. Title 45 ch.14](https://makecentsmakesense.nebraska.gov/sites/default/files/legal/Title-45_chapter-14_Livestock_Loans.pdf) (S) Texas examiners ask whether inspections are independent and documented. [Texas DOB](https://www.dob.texas.gov/public/uploads/files/Bank-Trust-Companies/Exam-Procedures/nrf14wk06.pdf) (S) No regulation forces spend on exit monitoring.

## 7. Unit-economics analogs

| Analog | Price |
|---|---|
| Alberta LIS alert, one year | C$52.50 ([LIS](https://lis-ab.com/information/client-alert-requests/)) |
| Montana brand lien filing | $25 per transaction, no annual fee ([MDOL](https://app.mt.gov/brandliens/Help/Instructions)) |
| ND agricultural lien buyer's report | $480 a year ([ND SOS](https://sos.nd.gov/node/4643)) (S) |
| Commercial UCC monitoring | Vendor prices unpublished. Forum posts claim $8-50 per entity per month ([Claimyr](https://claimyr.com/financial-services/ucc/Best-way-to-monitor-UCC-filings-for-portfolio-changes/2025-06-11)); anecdotal. |
| Pitch | $300-600 per loan per year, or $25-50 per month |

The pitch sits at the top of the UCC anecdote range and about 6-12x the two government alert and filing prices. A lender will pay a premium only if the alert prevents a loss. At $1M+ per loan, one prevented event pays for years, but base rates are unknown.

## 8. Is the why-now real?

- **True:** fall calf run timing; heifer retention (+1%) means more bred-heifer collateral.
- **Weak:** EID covers breeding-age cattle, not feeders. Price is falling about 20% from the April peak, which raises collateral shortfall pressure (my inference) but also borrower distress that tends to produce phantom-collateral fraud, which exit alerts do not catch.
- **Not supported:** that the 2026 fraud headline is an exit case (see Section 2).

## 9. Moat assessment

| Moat | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Network effects | Moderate, long-dated | Cold start on both sides; each barn needs enough lenders and vice versa |
| Switching costs | Weak | Lender profile upload is portable; a barn-software vendor or state portal could replicate it |
| Scale economies | Weak | Matching is cheap |
| Intangibles / data | Moderate | Pledge data is valuable only if lenders will share it, which has unresolved privacy and notice questions |

## 10. Gaps and what to test next

- **Interview first (10-15 lenders, 5 barns).** How often do lenders discover unauthorized sales, how do they find out, and what does a missed one cost? Is Sale Time's lien module actually used, and does it ingest lender data?
- **Pick a wedge outside brand-lien systems.** Montana and Nebraska already have lender channels. The Nebraska Sandhills and Kansas Flint Hills wedge needs a check on each state's brand and central-filing rules. I did not verify those.
- **Counsel questions:** FSA notice sufficiency, GLBA, and barn liability from receiving feeds.
- **Missing data:** current US market count; Sale Time customer count; lender losses by mechanism; the seven unconfirmed central-filing states; Nebraska lender-inspection fee amounts.
- **Reframe the pilot's success test:** require at least one real hit the lender did not know about. If the 4-week log shows zero, the thesis is dead.

# I0389-M1 Dossier: Scribe-Adjusted EBITDA (privileged diligence for physician deals)

Researched 2026-10-13 (about 40 searches and fetches). Tags: [P] primary or near-primary, [S] trade or secondary, [V] vendor marketing, [I] my inference or assumption. Where a page could not be fetched and I relied on a search snippet, I say so.

## Bottom line

The problem is real and buyers already pay outsiders for E/M coding review in physician-practice deals. But the idea as written is too small, too copyable, and its why-now is weaker than the finalist file claims.

1. Demand exists as a budget line, not as a new category. PYA, Aprio, VMG Health and HIA already sell coding review inside PE diligence. The new part is the scribe-specific causal framing.
2. My bottom-up count supports roughly 2 to 36 scribe-specific buy-side reports a year nationally (mid case about 10, roughly $0.3M). The plan assumes capacity of 50-100 reports a year.
3. Why-now is mixed. Payer downcoding is a patchwork of paused and live programs, and PE physician-practice deal counts have fallen by about half.
4. The staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) design is the one differentiated asset, and it is statistically fragile in groups of 20-150 providers [I].

Verdict: weak as a standalone venture (my score 4/10). Reasonable as a wedge inside a broader "E/M coding diligence for physician deals" practice, which is a different and more crowded business.

## 1. Is the why-now real?

**Evidence that scribes move coding.**
- Trilliant's six-system claims study (2018-2024) found high-intensity new-patient share up 12-20 points and established up 7-12 points. The authors say causes "are not clearly understood", the 2021 E/M rule changes may contribute, and the study is descriptive and does not isolate AI [P]. https://www.trillianthealth.com/market-research/studies/outpatient-coding-intensity-increases-as-hospitals-adopt-ai-enabled-scribing
- The best causal evidence is Holmgren et al. (JAMA Netw Open, January 2026): more than 1.2M encounters at one academic site, +5.8% weekly RVUs and +2.8% encounters per week, with no rise in denials. The authors cannot separate more services from better coding [P, via commentary]. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2843526 A UCSF summary describes a staggered-rollout DiD with volunteer early adopters (search snippet; page returned 403). https://docit.ucsf.edu/news/ucsf-study-finds-ai-scribes-associated-increased-physician-productivity-and-revenue
- BCBSA found an outlier inpatient maternity system where fewer than 20% of postpartum-anemia cases met clinical criteria. This is inpatient, not outpatient E/M [S]. https://hlth.com/insights/articles/how-ambient-ai-scribes-are-changing-medical-coding-intensity

**Payer downcoding is real but uneven.**
- Cigna R49 was announced for 10/1/2025, then "temporarily paused" pending California DMHC review [S]. https://streamlinemd.com/cigna-temporarily-pauses-its-e-m-coding-and-accuracy-policy/ A November 2025 AASM tracker lists Aetna and Cigna as implemented with no pause noted. https://aasm.org/growing-trend-of-downcoding-among-commercial-payers/ These conflict, and I could not resolve Cigna's current status. The finalist file's "Cigna's nationwide policy" is not safe to repeat.
- Anthem's policy (planned 2/15/2026) was paused repeatedly through at least 9/1/2026; I found nothing after that [S]. https://www.cmadocs.org/newsroom/news/view/ArticleId/51218/Anthem-extends-pause-on-E-M-downcoding-policy-through-Sept-1
- Centene/Ambetter is live: Cotiviti-run E/M leveling effective 7/15/2026 across Medicaid, Marketplace and Medicare (notice dated 4/23/2026) [P]. https://www.ambetterhealth.com/en/sc/provider-resources/provider-news/cotiviti-em-leveling-effective-july-2026/

**Enforcement climate.** DOJ FY2025 FCA recoveries were over $6.8B, with $5.7B healthcare and a record 1,297 qui tams [S]. https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/ I found no E/M upcoding FCA settlement tied to scribes. The article names no AI or EHR cases and says nothing on M&A diligence. OIG's February 2026 Medicare Advantage guidance warns about AI prompts that add risk-adjusting diagnoses; the alert does not address E/M [S]. https://www.parkerpoe.com/news/2026/06/oig-guidance-warns-physician-practices-of-compliance-risks

**Headwind: deal flow.** PitchBook counts PE physician-practice-management deals falling from 851 (2021) to 105 in H1 2026, on pace for about half of 2025, with over a dozen states adding PE oversight laws [S, paywalled]. https://statnews.com/2026/08/17/private-equity-50-percent-drop-physician-practice-management-deals-2026 Fifteen states had transaction-notice laws by 1/30/2026 [S]. https://bassberry.com/news/how-dealmakers-should-prepare-amid-state-legislatures-targeting-healthcare-private-equity-investments/ Longer state review could lengthen deal timelines, which may help diligence but shrinks volume [I].

**Net:** the drift is documented, the payer response is partial, and the buyer pool is shrinking. The claim that "this diligence item did not exist in 2023" is true for scribes but misleading, since E/M coding diligence has existed for years.

## 2. Competitors and incumbents

| Player | What they sell | Traction / funding | Threat |
|---|---|---|---|
| VMG Health | Buy-side diligence for a PE-backed MSO buying a 30+ physician ophthalmology practice: CPT utilization by provider plus chart audit; buyer adjusted purchase agreements (no dollar figures). Also Compliance Risk Analyzer and AI-governance audits. https://vmghealth.com/case-studies/guiding-success-in-new-markets-buy-side-due-diligence-in-ophthalmology/ | Private; no funding data | High. Already in the buyer's seat; no scribe SKU found |
| PYA | Coding reviews for PE buyers; a principal said requests rose over "three to four years" (2019 quote). https://www.pyapc.com/insights/pya-principal-quoted-in-recent-article-on-private-equity-and-due-diligence-in-healthcare/ | Private | High |
| Aprio | Sept 2024 case: 150+ provider ENT/allergy network; Level V visits about 70% above national; office-visit revenue (about 75% of total) overstated about 25%; used to adjust price. No sample size or fee. https://aprio.com/case-study-unlocking-value-in-healthcare-private-equity-with-data-driven-transactional-due-diligence-ins-article-he | Private | High. Best proof buyers act on E/M findings |
| HIA | Due-diligence coding audit; 1-2 weeks plus 1-2 weeks to report; price on request. https://hiacode.com/due-diligence-audits | Private | Medium. Cheap generalist |
| Guidehouse/Navigant | Pre-acquisition E/M and modifier benchmarking against Medicare claims (2018 PDF). https://guidehouse.com/-/media/www/site/downloads/healthcare/2018/navigant-pre-acquisition-assessments.pdf?la=en | Large consultancy | Medium |
| MDaudit, Healthicity, Cotiviti | In-house compliance and payer-side software. MDaudit launched Auditor Assist 7/15/2026; no scribe-specific product found. https://mdaudit.com/news/mdaudit-advances-its-meaningful-ai-strategy-with-the-addition-of-auditor-assist-to-its-continuous-risk-monitoring-solutions-suite/ | Not found | Low-medium; could add a module |
| Scribe vendors | Abridge (about $5.3B at a June 2025 round; secondary estimates $5.7-7.0B) https://trueup.io/co/abridge; Ambience ($243M Series C, $1.25B, July 2025) https://fiercehealthcare.com/health-tech/ambience-banks-243m-series-c-investors-continue-bet-big-ambient-ai; DeepScribe (about $40M total) https://www.cbinsights.com/company/deepscribe/financials | Menlo: ambient documentation about $600M of $1.4B 2025 healthcare AI spend; 67% of outpatient scribe users expect to switch vendors within three years https://healthexec.com/topics/artificial-intelligence/healthcare-ai-spending-unitedhealth-ai-claims-processing | They self-attest. Vendor churn means mixed-vendor histories, so scribe-agnostic is a real feature |
| Free academic benchmarks | Johns Hopkins (Dai, Polsky) NIHCM grant through 12/2026 https://nihcm.org/grantees/ambient-ai-documentation-and-billing-intensity-evidence-from-commercial-claims; Trilliant; Holmgren | Public | Will commoditize the "typical uplift by vendor and specialty" benchmark moat |

I found no startup selling a scribe-specific diligence product, but two extended searches turned up mostly listicles, so coverage is imperfect. The finalist file's "nobody sells a coder-signed audit in diligence" is wrong for generic E/M diligence; it holds only for the scribe-cohort causal framing. VMG, PYA and Aprio could add that framing in a quarter [I].

## 3. Bottom-up market size

Anchors: the deal-count anchors are the PitchBook counts above, plus a Bass Berry tally of 367 PPM transactions through Q3 2025 (all buyers, from a snippet; page returned 403) https://beckersasc.com/asc-transactions-and-valuation-issues/private-equity-eyes-physician-practice-deals-in-2025.html. Staggered rollouts do create controls, and the academic literature uses this design (Holmgren, one academic system, 1.2M+ encounters). A 30-provider group with perhaps 10-20 adopters, volunteer early adopters and rollout timing correlated with provider productivity gives wide confidence intervals and selection bias [I]. ## Bottom line

The policy shock is real and dated, but the evidence supports a narrow service business, not the pitch's $1.15M year-one story. Five findings drive that:

1. The "documentation wall" is later and softer than pitched (section 1).
2. Nebraska's first coverage losses are mostly non-response, not missing proof.

## 1. Why-now check: real, but later and softer

The $580 monthly income path (minimum wage x 80 hours) and combining activities are both allowed (same source).
- [F] The look-back is 1-3 months at application, plus at least one month since the last renewal, and the state chooses ([SHVS](https://shvs.org/resources/cms-releases-interim-final-rule-on-medicaid-work-reporting-requirements/)).
- [F] In CY2027 states may require documentation or accept auditable self-declaration. From 2028 they must require documentation when reasonably available. If it does not exist, states must accept "other sufficient information" and cannot deny solely for missing documents. States define what counts as sufficient (SHVS, same page). AAMC asked CMS to extend self-attestation ([AAMC](https://www.aamc.org/advocacy-policy/washington-highlights/aamc-raises-concern-over-medicaid-community-engagement-interim-final-rule)).

- [F] Nebraska has been live since May 1. It mails a notice plus a declaration form due in 30 days. Through Aug 2026, 14% of 4,089 new applicants subject to the rule were denied (557), and 7% of 7,280 renewals lost coverage (533). Of those, 84% and 92% respectively were non-response, and only 16% and 8% were affirmatively found noncompliant ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/medicaid/early-medicaid-work-requirement-insights-from-nebraska/)). # I0996-M1 Dossier: ERCOT Large-Load Energization Files, Fixed Fee

Research date: 2026-10-13. Method: ERCOT primary documents (rule text, impact analyses, board decks, stakeholder comments) plus targeted web search. Pricing and competitor traction data were largely not findable; gaps are flagged.

## Verdict

**Conditional go, but re-aim.** The regulatory pull is real and larger than the pitch says, but it comes from a different rule than the one the pitch leads with. Three corrections matter:

1. **NOGRR282 does not create the acceptance gate.** It is a performance rule enforced after a trip event. The gate is **PGRR144**, which is recommended for approval but not confirmed approved by the PUCT.
2. **The "no direct competitor" finding is wrong.** At least four consultancies already market ERCOT large-load model services. None showed a hardware-validated, reusable library, but none disclosed pricing either.
3. **The OEM is the biggest threat.** ERCOT itself says converter validation is "generally performed in OEM's lab" and "usually performed once" per converter family. That supports the reuse thesis and also invites OEMs to cut out the middleman.

Near-term cash timing is also worse than assumed. The Texas governor's data center audit paused energization approvals for 75 MW and larger data centers on Aug 3, 2026.

## 1. What the rules actually require

**NOGRR282** (effective Aug 1, 2026; [ERCOT page](https://www.ercot.com/mktrules/issues/NOGRR282)):
- It sets voltage and frequency ride-through tables for Large Computational Loads (LCLs), defined as Large Loads of 75 MW or more where 50% or more of site demand is power-electronic computational load (definition quoted in search results from the [NPRR1308 PRS report](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2025/12/14/1308NPRR-06-PRS-Report-121025.docx); the ERCOT issue page does not restate it).
- The text has no model submission, test report or pre-energization evidence requirement. Enforcement is reactive: if ERCOT finds a failed ride-through, the customer has 90 days for a root-cause report, 90 days for a plan and 180 days to implement. ERCOT may order disconnection for imminent risk ([original text](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2025/11/14/282NOGRR-01-Large-Electronic-Load-Ride-Through-Requirements-111425.docx); [PUCT-approved redline](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/07/11/282NOGRR-45-PUCT-Report-070926.docx)).
- Grandfathering is broad: loads with approval to energize, or executed agreements and study completion, by mid-2026 are exempt ([PUCT redline](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/07/11/282NOGRR-45-PUCT-Report-070926.docx)).

**PGRR144** is the real forcing function ([ERCOT page](https://www.ercot.com/mktrules/issues/PGRR144)). ROS recommended it on 7/9/26, TAC on 8/26/26 with 3 opposed and 4 abstaining, and the Board on 9/15/26. I found no PUCT order. It takes effect the first of the month after PUCT approval ([TAC report](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/08/31/144PGRR-19-TAC-Report-082626.docx)). It would require:
- Dynamic models in PSS/E, PSCAD and TSAT.
- Model quality tests for all Large Loads (flat start and large voltage disturbance).
- For LCLs, a **converter model validation** report benchmarking the PSCAD model against hardware tests.
- As-built models plus an owner attestation before initial energization.
- Re-review through the interconnection study for any material LCL change.

([ERCOT 6/11/26 comments](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/06/11/144PGRR-11-ERCOT-Comments-061126.docx))

Details that shape the business:
- ERCOT's pre-energization review ends in "approved, or additional information required." ERCOT rejected a Data Center Coalition request to delete that approval language ([ERCOT responses](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/06/18/PGRR144-ERCOT-responses-to-DCC-comments_June2026.pdf)). A real acceptance event exists.
- ERCOT states that completing the tests "does not constitute an endorsement" of NOGRR282 compliance ([ERCOT/ESIG deck](https://www.esig.energy/attachment/serve/ercot-modeling-requirements-and-mqt_june2026_esig_workshop)). Acceptance and compliance are separate things.
- Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) is an accepted validation method. It is usually done in the OEM's lab, once per converter family ([same deck](https://www.esig.energy/attachment/serve/ercot-modeling-requirements-and-mqt_june2026_esig_workshop)). The draft text says IBR inverter validation results "can be submitted for multiple uses of that model," and describes the LCL converter test the same way, as a hardware-type benchmark of converter components rather than a site test ([ERCOT comments](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/06/11/144PGRR-11-ERCOT-Comments-061126.docx)).
- Dynamics data is "Protected Information," so accepted submissions never become public precedent.

## 2. Is the why-now real?

**Yes on regulation, mixed on timing.**
- Dynamic models already gate queue position. Of Batch Zero loads, 47 were removed for submitting no dynamic model by July 10 ([ERCOT 8/19/26 deck](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/08/19/ERCOTPanel1DataCenters.pdf)). Some are conditionally included "subject to curing deficiencies in dynamic model data" ([Board deck 9/14-15](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/09/11/14-Batch-Zero-Update.pdf)).
- ERCOT's own PSCAD open-source data center model "has not been validated against actual hardware" ([ERCOT/TAMU manual](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/04/24/Dynamic-Modeling-of-AI-Data-Center-Load-in-PSCAD-Manual.pdf)). A Sandia briefing to ERCOT says ERCOT "still requires hardware-validated EMT models with real control loops" ([Sandia deck](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/09/04/4-Voltage-and-Frequency-Ride-through-for-large-computational-loads-State-of-the-Art.pdf)).
- NERC issued a Level 3 alert on May 4, 2026 and proposed registering "Computational Load Entities" at 20 MW and up. That widens the opportunity beyond ERCOT ([DWT summary](https://www.dwt.com/blogs/energy--environmental-law-blog/2026/05/nerc-level-3-alert-large-loads-data-centers)).

**Headwinds:**
- **Energization freeze.** On Aug 3, 2026 ERCOT paused approvals to energize data centers and crypto sites of 75 MW or more. The verification report is due Dec 10, 2026, and the impact on Batch Zero timing is "TBD" ([Board deck](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/09/11/14-Batch-Zero-Update.pdf); [market notice](https://www.ercot.com/services/comm/mkt_notices/M-A080326-01)). Expect cash slippage of roughly two quarters.
- **Closed on-ramp.** The legacy study process closed to new submissions July 10 ([Board deck](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/09/11/14-Batch-Zero-Update.pdf)). Ongoing batches await a future rule ([Mondaq](https://www.mondaq.com/unitedstates/oil-gas-electricity/1807826/puct-approves-batch-zero-framework-that-will-provide-a-pathway-for-large-load-to-connect-to-the-grid-and-receive-electricity)). The "first wave hitting the queue now" claim is stale. The buyer pool is mostly Batch Zero, not new entrants.
- **Size mismatch.** The 25-300 MW wedge overlaps the rules only at 75 MW and above. Sites of 25-75 MW get only a community-impact data request ([Board deck](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/09/11/14-Batch-Zero-Update.pdf)).

## 3. Bottom-up market size

- Batch Zero conditionally includes **362 projects, about 194 GW** (204 base, 66.4 GW; 158 studied, 127.9 GW), an average near 540 MW per project ([Board deck](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/09/11/14-Batch-Zero-Update.pdf)). Queue totals vary by source and date: 410, 438, 445.8 and 474 GW appear in different documents.
- No source gives a size split. **Assumption:** 20-30% are 75-300 MW sites owned by developers with no in-house power-electronics staff. That is about 70-110 projects.
- At $150k per package, the one-time pool is roughly **$10-16M**. Re-issue at $20-40k per year adds **$1.5-4M per year**.
- The pitch's 12 packages in year 1 would be 11-17% of that pool, which is aggressive for a new shop facing a freeze. **My estimate:** 4-8 packages, or $0.4-1.2M, in the first 12 months.
- The audit covers roughly 250-300 projects, about 200 GW (figure from a search summary of ERCOT/Pillsbury material, not confirmed in the fetched deck; [Pillsbury](https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/texas-data-center-interconnections-audit-gate-governor-abbott-directive-update.html)). Conditional classifications can be revoked if a project fails the audit or a quarterly stability assessment.

## 4. Evidence of demand and willingness to pay

**Strong (forcing functions and stakes):**
- Delay value. BloombergNEF prices a slip at about $175M per GW-month for conventional cloud and $1.76B per GW-month for AI compute ([MGRID summary](https://mgrid.org/?p=16192)). That is $0.18M to $1.76M per MW-month, so the pitch's $100/kW-month ($0.1M per MW) is conservative. It is deferred revenue, not loss.
- Adjacent state fees. The proposed rules under Texas SB6 include study fees of $100-300k and $50k per MW security ([Foley](https://www.foley.com/insights/publications/2026/03/public-utility-commission-of-texas-issues-proposed-rules-for-large-load-interconn/)). That is a proposal, not final.
- Sandia estimates one-time costs of **$1-15M** to reach ride-through compliance with a grid-interactive UPS and **$25-90M** for E-STATCOM or battery solutions, per 100 MW. A $150k model package is about 1% or less of that spend. The larger money is in design and mitigation.
- Developers accept the model requirement. Hut 8 told ERCOT it is "comfortable with a requirement to provide accurate models" but fears restudy risk ([Hut 8 comments](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/03/03/144PGRR-03-Hut-8-Comments-030326.docx)). It argued GPU fleets may eventually shed UPS, which could shrink the ride-through hardware base.

**Absent:** RFPs, quoted consultant prices, forum complaints about cost or backlog for large-load models. No transaction price was found for a PSCAD data center model or validation. The only rate signal is a UK EMT consultant posting at £650-800 per day ([job listing](https://www.mane.co.uk/job/power-system-engineer-)). Demand is regulatory, and **paid demand remains unproven**.

## 5. Competitive landscape

Industry metrics (Step 0): days from model kickoff to ERCOT sign-off, resubmittal loops, MW cleared, price per package and gross margin.

No pricing, headcount or named clients | **High**: same offer |

**Moat assessment:**
- Network effects: weak.
- Switching costs: moderate, from as-built re-issue and OEM NDA relationships.
- Scale economies: moderate, from reusing a converter-family validation across sites.
- Intangibles: weak to moderate. ERCOT's Dynamics Working Group publishes the test procedures, and submissions are confidential, so tacit knowledge diffuses slowly but is not protected.

**Structural vulnerability:** OEMs hold the control details and can validate once for all their customers.

**Durable edge:** an independent lab-validated library covering multiple OEMs, plus speed with ERCOT reviewers.

## 6. Unit economics

- **Assumption:** a fully loaded engineer costs about $250 per hour, so a $150k package funds about 600 hours.
- If reused platform models cut site-specific work to 250-300 hours, **gross margin is roughly 50-60%** before HIL lab and NDA costs. Without reuse it is about the 30-40% consultancy norm.
- ERCOT's Dynamic Studies group estimates 1,700 hours per year for ride-through and model review ([impact analysis](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/04/14/282NOGRR-25-Revised-Impact-Analysis-041426.docx)). Review capacity looks thin, so resubmittal loops may be the real bottleneck. This is my inference.
- Pricing anchor check: $90-180k is plausible against the stakes above. No competitor price exists to benchmark.

## 7. Regulatory and liability landscape

- The attestation that as-built data matches field settings belongs to the developer. A bad model's consequences (restudy, disconnection) flow to the developer, who may look to the consultant. E&O insurance is needed (not researched).
- Texas requires engineering firms to register with TBPELS and name a supervising P.E. ([TBPELS fee schedule](https://pels.texas.gov/fees.htm)).
- The 25% success kicker needs care. NSPE's code bars contingent compensation "under circumstances in which their judgment may be compromised," though contingency is not per se unethical ([NSPE](https://www.nspe.org/career-growth/ethics/board-ethical-review-cases/expert-witness-services)). I did not find the Texas rule text, so get counsel to confirm. Structuring it as a milestone fee rather than a findings-contingent fee is safer.
- OEM NDAs are the binding constraint on the reusable-library plan. The rule text treats validation as reusable, but access to OEM hardware and control firmware is commercial.

## 8. Scenarios, kill criteria and next steps

| Scenario | Probability (my judgment) | Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Bull | 20% | PGRR144 approved as written. OEMs outsource validation to independents. Year-1 revenue above $1.5M. |
| Base | 45% | PGRR144 approved. A few developers buy gap analyses and packages. Revenue $0.4-1.2M, slower than planned because of the freeze. |
| Bear | 35% | OEMs self-serve or the PUCT waters down converter validation. Existing consultancies price low. Shop becomes a bespoke consultancy. |

**Kill triggers:**
- The PUCT rejects or materially weakens the converter-validation requirement in PGRR144.
- Two of three major UPS OEMs say they will supply validated PSCAD models and ERCOT-ready validation reports free to customers.
- Fewer than three developers agree to pay at least $60k in the first 30 days.

**Re-aimed first 30 days:**
1. Pull the PUCT docket for PGRR144 and confirm its status and effective date.
2. Call 3-5 Batch Zero developers at 75-300 MW. Ask who built their July 10 models, what it cost and which "cure deficiency" notices they received.
3. Ask two UPS OEMs and one power-shelf maker whether they will provide PSCAD models with validation reports, and whether they would license a third party to validate.
4. Price-check Keentel, PSC and ZEG by requesting a quote.

## Gaps and confidence

- High confidence: rule text and process facts (primary ERCOT documents).
- Not found: PUCT action on PGRR144, any consultant price, OEM model-validation plans, the size split of Batch Zero projects, Typhoon and OPAL-RT funding, and the Texas contingent-fee rule text.
- Note: the PUCT-approved NOGRR282 is a merged redline, so exact final thresholds should be re-read in the clean Operating Guide text.
- Sources conflict on queue size and terminology (LEL versus LCL).

objections: The proposed wedge market is the most incumbent-saturated place to start, and the product is a thin layer over tools that already exist at the same chokepoints. Nebraska (Sandhills) has a certified central filing system where lenders file an effective financing statement (EFS) and registered buyers and commission merchants receive the master lien list for a small registration fee (about $30 plus per-list fees; sources conflict). It also has mandatory brand inspection in the western two-thirds of the state, with ownership proof required at every sale barn. Under Neb. Rev. Stat. 54-1,100 the Brand Committee will not record a brand transfer once the lender has noticed a lien, unless the lender consents. The 2026 attempt to abolish mandatory inspection (LB1258) stalled after a six-hour hearing, and a compromise (LB1187) was signed instead, so this chokepoint is politically entrenched. Montana already has a $25-per-filing lender portal, and Alberta sells a C$52.50 a year alert. A state agency or a barn-software vendor can add alerts at zero marginal price, and they have statutory reach over every barn in the state. A startup depends on voluntary barn participation.

The supply side and the lender workflow are both owned by someone else, and the matching logic is a commodity. Sale Time Systems (founded 1988) already runs check-in, lien verification, brand management and settlement inside the barn and is co-developing an ownership module with Washington's agriculture department. I found no lender-facing feed, but it could ship one in a sprint, and ViewTrak claims 400+ locations. The Livestock Marketing Association (LMA) claims 85% of markets, already sells members legal help on lien law, and built its own shared payment-risk service (PAYS) in 2015. It can bundle a free lien-clearing feature for members, or gate the barns' data and demand a cut. On the lender side, Farmers National Company already does SOC-1-compliant collateral inspections for banks (about 400,000 head per quarter, 12 states, reports regulators like). Abrigo and Nortridge own loan servicing. The dossier's own moat table calls scale economies weak and switching costs weak, because a lender profile upload is portable. The 'cornered resource' claim only holds if lenders hand over pledge data in bulk to a vendor with no distribution of its own.

The strongest competitor is lender inertia and cheap substitutes, which caps price and demand. A Baird Holm lender-side article calls filing an EFS or sending direct notices 'easy and inexpensive' and 'cheap insurance', yet notes lenders under-use it because they believe other safeguards suffice. Lenders also already use joint-payee checks, assignment of proceeds, advance-notice-of-sale covenants and annual inspections. If banks skip a roughly $30 tool they know about, a $300-600 per loan per year alert is a hard sell. Pain is low: Fed farmland charge-offs were 0.01-0.03% in 2025, farm delinquency was about 1.3%, and livestock concern in the Farmer Mac survey was at its record low. The cases I found were detected by physical counts, defaults, family complaints or a packer (Tyson), not by watching exits. The dossier already shows the price is 6-12x the government anchors, and the 'phantom collateral' fraud type is not caught by exit alerts at all. Pilot reality check: the 4-week test needs a real undisclosed hit, and the base rate of such hits is unknown.

The product is easiest to evade for exactly the borrowers who commit fraud, and the incumbents with legal mandate cover leakage that a voluntary network cannot. In the Kentucky Cox case (about $1.1M of pledged cattle sold), the borrower sold under a fake farm name ('High Ridge') at locations the lender had not approved, specifically so buyers could not check pledge status with the credit association. A name-matching alert fails when the alias is unknown to the lender, and only covers barns that joined. About 31% of feeder and stocker receipts bypass auction barns (direct about 16%, video or internet about 15%), fed cattle go feedyard to packer, and barns are closing. The network-effect moat takes years to form, while the product is incomplete the whole time. Also, Packers and Stockyards rules (9 CFR 201.43) require a market to remit net proceeds to the consignor by the close of the next business day, so a 'joint-check prompt' leaves little room for a barn to hold money on a third-party alert. Barns also gain protection under 7 U.S.C. 1631(g) by not receiving formal notice, which reduces their incentive to participate.

The Phase 3 title-registry expansion, the only path to a venture-scale outcome, runs into incumbents with legal authority or deep pockets and a history of producer rejection. State brand registries are the legally recognized proof of ownership, and cattle have no title statute. USDA's NAIS cost over $120M, reached only about 36% participation, and was scrapped in 2010 over privacy and cost objections. The Nov 2024 EID rule covers only breeding-age, dairy and exhibition cattle, so feeder calves remain untagged. Tag and sensor owners (Merck/Allflex/Vence, Gallagher, and Halter at a $2B valuation after a $220M Series E in March 2026) hold per-animal data, and Brazil shows the incumbent template: B3 exchange plus Cowmed collars registering livestock-backed loans. Lender-funded neutrality is the stated counter, but the buyers (about 280 relevant ag banks by the dossier's estimate) are too few and small to fund a registry. The dossier's own sizing is $1.5-6M ARR at 20-30% penetration for Phase 1.

objections: PRICE EXCEEDS THE LOSS THE PRODUCT CAN PREVENT, AND NOTHING FORCES THE SPEND. The pitch charges lenders $300-600 per loan per year. Net charge-offs on ag production loans at all US commercial banks averaged about 0.165% annualized over the last 12 quarters (range 0.05-0.29%), and 'negligible' at all but the largest ag banks per the KC Fed. On an assumed $500K cattle loan, ALL-cause expected net loss (crop failure, divorce, price drops, fraud) is about $825/yr, or roughly $400-500 at the 0.08-0.10% reported for banks outside the top 100. The exit-sale mechanism is a small slice of that. The dossier found only 2 of about 8 documented cases that fit 'pledged cattle sold, proceeds kept', both small. If exit-sale is 5-15% of losses (my assumption), the expected-loss value of the alert is about $20-125/loan/yr ($40-250 on a $1M loan), against a $300-600 price. The dossier also found no regulation requiring exit monitoring and no RFPs. Public price anchors (Alberta LIS alert C$52.50/yr, Montana brand lien $25/filing, North Dakota statewide lien master list $480/yr for the whole state) sit 6-12x below the ask. Lenders already have a near-free substitute, joint-payee checks and written notice, and a Nebraska banking article shows one bank skipping it as 'too much trouble'. A pain whose cheap fix is already ignored is not urgent. The best counter-evidence is anecdotal forum posts of UCC monitoring at $20-50/entity/month, which suggests risk-averse lenders may pay above expected loss. That is one unverified data point. Repricing to $50-100 shrinks the Phase 1 pool to roughly $0.8-1.3M ARR at 20-30% penetration.

THE DATA SUPPLIER (THE SALE BARN) HAS NO BUDGET AND A NEGATIVE INCENTIVE. Under 7 USC 1631(g)(1) a commission merchant or selling agent takes free of the seller's security interest even if the interest is perfected and the agent knows of it. The protection is lost only on written notice within the prior year with unmet payment conditions, or on non-registration or a Secretary of State notice in central-filing states. A barn that ingests lender pledge feeds and sends alerts is volunteering to become a noticed party and giving up a statutory shield, in exchange for a 'free lien check' it already gets from its clerking software (Sale Time Systems advertises lien verification) and from statutory master lists. So the free tier is not a gift to the barn, it is a liability, and the barn's lawyer or liability insurer is the likely blocker. The follow-on ask of $200-500/month ($2.4-6K/yr) is 5-12x the $480/yr North Dakota statewide master list. Barn economics are poor: one Oregon/Washington barn's commissions are flat while labor, insurance and repairs roughly tripled in 8 years, and volumes are falling. TrustBIX, parent of ViewTrak (which claimed 400+ auction locations), saw revenue fall about 42-45% in the periods reported and classified ViewTrak as a discontinued operation by Dec 2025. That is weak evidence barns pay real money for software. The whole premise that barns email pre-sale consignment lists to a third party is unverified. I found no evidence of barns sharing seller names with lenders, and the legal consignor-record requirements I found exist for regulators only. Without barn data there is no product, and the cold start needs 8-12 barns and 10-20 lenders in one region, both lukewarm.

THE GO-TO-MARKET MATH FAILS: SMALL ACV, SLOW AND FRAGMENTED BUYERS, UNCLEAR SIGNER. The pitch's own week-4 ask is $300/loan x a 20-loan minimum, so the entry deal is $6K/yr. Selling to community banks means vendor due diligence under the 2023 interagency third-party risk guidance (a startup with no references, no SOC report, and a data-sharing product handling borrower names). The only timing evidence I found is anecdotal (fintech executives cite 12-18 months from procurement to implementation), but it consistently points to long cycles. A $6K-45K ACV on a 12-month-plus, relationship-driven cycle with rural field sales almost certainly has CAC above first-year revenue (my inference; no CAC data exists for this niche). The buyer pool is shrinking: ag banks reportedly down about 66% since 1994, Farm Credit System down from about 900 entities to 71, and the big cattle lenders (Rabo, CoBank, AgriBank) run their own audit teams. The champion (the loan officer) bears the cost: every alert creates a call to a good customer, and fuzzy matching on common ranch family names and relatives selling legitimately will produce false positives and alert fatigue. The budget owner (credit administration or compliance) sees no regulatory driver. The realistic five-year outcome is the dossier's own $1.5-6M ARR ceiling with no confirmed path to the Phase 3 registry.

THE DEMAND EVIDENCE DOES NOT MATCH THE PRODUCT, SO THE PILOT WILL MISREAD INTEREST. The documented cattle-collateral losses were found by other means: Rabo/McClain ($50.6M) surfaced from a collapse in borrower-reported inventory (89,522 to 37,992 head) and an on-site audit, not from a barn alert, and the Texas, Decatur and Missouri bank-VP cases were phantom collateral or insider fraud, which exit alerts cannot catch. Where sales were detected (Knudsen, Peplinski, Cox, Arkansas), it was through inspections, loan-covenant violations, missed payments or a family complaint, the existing toolset. Free pilots with friendly lenders will produce enthusiasm without payment evidence. 'We would like to know' is not budget. The pitch's headline fraud (the $2.8M/850-head case) is, per the dossier, a forged bill of sale by a bank VP, with no liens or barns involved, so the why-now story is a mismatch. Market conditions cut the other way: the herd is at a 75-year low, barns are closing, and prices are down about 20% from the May 2026 peak.

THE MOAT AND PRICING POWER ARE ILLUSORY BECAUSE THE FREE ALTERNATIVES ARE ONE FEATURE AWAY. Sale Time Systems already has lien verification in the barn workflow and a state agency (WSDA) is co-developing brand-ownership verification inside it. Montana already runs a lender-facing brand lien portal at $25 per filing, and Alberta runs a statutory alert service at C$52.50. Any of these can add an alert and set the market price at zero. The 'cornered resource' claim (lender pledge data) is circular: lenders will share borrower data with a startup only if it has barn coverage, and barns will join only if lenders are loaded. Lender data sharing carries unresearched GLBA, state data-law and negligence-claim risks (a missed alert before a loss invites blame), which push bank counsel toward 'no'. Phase 3 (a title registry) is a public-good institution that other countries run via regulators or exchanges (Kenya, Mongolia, B3 in Brazil). A private US startup would be asking lenders, packers and brand agencies to pay a toll and trust a neutral they did not fund.

objections: The 'gap' is mostly an artifact of framing. Buy-side E/M coding review inside physician-practice diligence is already a served, budgeted service, and the incumbents already hold the buyer-counsel-underwriter relationships this plan needs. PYA lists 'Coding and Billing Compliance Reviews' under its transaction services and a principal says buyer requests have grown. HIA sells a diligence coding audit in about 1-2 weeks plus 1-2 weeks to report. VMG and Aprio have published buy-side cases where E/M findings changed price. Mid-market RWI underwriters reportedly already require a chart audit by a reputable firm before they will cover billing and coding, so the buyer's default is the incumbent they already know. The only differentiator is the staggered difference-in-differences framing, and that is an analysis step. PYA, VMG or Aprio can add it as a line item at near-zero marginal cost and bundle it into an engagement the buyer is already paying for. The finalist file's own competition note concedes incumbents could rebrand it 'within a quarter or two'. The disruptive-innovation question, why incumbents will rationally NOT respond, has no good answer here. There is no cannibalization, no channel conflict and no regulatory barrier. A $20-45k add-on also competes with a $25-75k QoE, so the QoE or coding-review firm will absorb it into its own scope. Calling QoE firms 'channel partners, not rivals' is wishful, because they are the ones who can fold it in and undercut it.

Funded AI-native auditors already do scribe-aware E/M auditing at 100% coverage with a financial guarantee, and the research missed them. Brellium (reported $16.7M Series A led by First Round) audits E/M level and charge capture, says it audits 'the notes your Scribe produces', published a 2025 AI Scribe Compliance Report, is EHR-agnostic, and offers a clawback guarantee ('if a Brellium approved document triggers a clawback, Brellium will cover it'). Charta Health ($8.1M seed led by Bain Capital Ventures) reviews 100% of pre-bill charts. HIA (a cheap generalist coder shop) already markets an 'AI Validation Audit' and, per its AI services list, performance monitoring and trend analysis. Harine Management markets 'Due Diligence Analytics' and practice analytics to PE firms and already tells the same 'ambient scribe causes 99214/99215 drift in the first 90 days' story. These tools undercut the economics of 150-300 coder-reviewed encounters at 30-45 coder hours per report. They can also sit inside the target after close, which kills the planned $4-8k/month 100-day monitor upsell, and Brellium's guarantee is something a two-person services shop cannot match. Caveat: I found no evidence that Brellium or Charta sell into M&A diligence today (their pages never mention PE or diligence). The risk is that adding it is a one-sprint product decision for them, and a PE-owned MSO is a natural customer after close.

Every asset the plan calls a moat is commoditizing or copyable. (a) The free 'public-data pre-screen' lead magnet uses public CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners data, and the method is already taught publicly (AAPC has a CMS-based E/M benchmarking tool), so any competitor analyst can copy it and offer it free to win the whole paid engagement. (b) The 'cross-deal benchmark of typical uplift by scribe vendor and specialty' is being produced for free by Johns Hopkins (NIHCM grant through 12/2026), Trilliant, and UCSF/Holmgren. The deal count needed to build a proprietary version is about 10 a year at the mid case, so it never reaches data scale. (c) Auditing scribe output with LLM pipelines is going open: Composo released the prompts, pipeline and benchmark for an AI-scribe note audit instrument (it does not cover E/M codes, so this is a trend signal, not a direct substitute). That pushes coder-hour cost, the actual delivery bottleneck, toward zero for anyone with an LLM stack, and weakens the 'coder-signed' differentiator. (d) The staggered DiD is the single differentiated idea, and the dossier itself rates it statistically fragile at 20-150 providers. Methods consultancies can replicate a fragile method quickly, and the first buyer burned by a wide confidence interval will go back to the incumbent. 7 Powers read: no scale economies at about 10 deals a year, no network effect, no switching costs (one-time project), no cornered resource. Only counter-positioning is claimed, and it is thin because incumbents lose nothing by copying.

Distribution is held by incumbents, and the reputational risk lands on the person hiring you. The plan's buyer is the deal counsel, who needs a consultant whose number can anchor an $8M price adjustment or escrow and survive scrutiny from the investment committee, RWI underwriter and seller. Counsel already have go-to healthcare consultants (PYA, VMG, Aprio). A brand-new two-person firm has no track record, no references and no underwriter acceptance, and the pilot is priced at $12-15k in exchange for a reference. Privilege is also weaker than the pitch implies: Kovel protection is narrow, and work used mainly to reprice a deal often is not protected, especially if the report goes to lenders or the RWI underwriter. The report's value (a number the IC uses) pulls against its privilege. Sellers can also pre-empt with a sell-side coding review from a familiar firm, or hand over scribe-vendor 'AAPC-verified' compliance claims (Ambience markets 90-100% E/M accuracy, AAPC audited), which gives buyer-side incumbents an easy 'sufficient comfort' path. Epic's native AI Charting (launched Feb 2026) bundled with its revenue-cycle AI could further centralize scribe, coding and audit logs inside the EHR vendor. I could not confirm that Epic offers E/M suggestions or a benchmark, so treat that as unverified.

The space incumbents would have to defend is small and shrinking, so a startup cannot live in the niche incumbents ignore. They do not have to ignore it, because they can serve it as an add-on. Bottom-up demand is about 2-36 scribe-specific buy-side reports a year (mid case about 10, roughly $0.3M), against planned capacity of 50-100. PitchBook counts PE physician-practice-management deals falling from 851 (2021) to 105 in H1 2026, roughly -46% to -50% year over year, with state transaction-review laws spreading. Health Capital notes add-ons remain plentiful, but those are $8-12k add-on projects where the generalist coding shops are cheapest. Payer downcoding, the why-now for 'uplift won't persist', is a patchwork: Cigna R49 was announced for 10/1/2025 then paused pending California DMHC review, Anthem is paused, and I found nothing dated 2026 confirming a live Cigna or Aetna commercial E/M program. Only Centene via Cotiviti is confirmed live. Cotiviti's payer-side leveling is also the de facto definition of 'supported', so a coder-signed opinion that disagrees with the payer's algorithm gets discounted. Net: at best a $0.3-1M a year boutique, which is a feature of PYA/VMG/Aprio's existing practice, not a separate company.

objections: BARNS HAVE NO REASON TO FEED IT, AND SOME REASON NOT TO. The plan needs auction markets to hand over pre-sale consignor lists for free. But 7 U.S.C. 1631(g) already protects a commission merchant unless it was formally noticed or failed to register in a central-filing state (the dossier covers this). Meanwhile 9 CFR 201.43(a) lets a market agency pay the consignor by the next business day only 'in the absence of any knowledge that any other person, or persons, has any interest in the livestock.' A market that ingests lender profiles gains knowledge, loses that clean payout path, takes on joint-payee clearing work, delays its own sellers (who can then consign to the next barn), and builds a discoverable record for conversion suits. Free product plus legal downside plus competitive downside equals counsel-driven refusal. The barns that agree will be the careful ones; the barns cheating borrowers actually use will not join (adverse selection). The dossier also treats 'the barn emails the consignment list before sale day' as given. I found no evidence that commercial barns publish seller names or consignment lists ahead of sale (breed and video-auction catalogs are public, barn sales are different), and many lots arrive sale morning. If lists arrive after the sale, the alert is a post-mortem. The AgCountry v. Tri-County case (Minnesota) shows the real failure mode: the lender alleged the barn did not check or disregarded its effective financing statement on the state master list. The data existed; barn diligence was the gap, and this product does not fix that.

THE LENDER BUYER IS EITHER ALREADY PROTECTED OR TOO SLOPPY TO BUY. A Texas banker's own description of normal practice (TSCRA Ask a Banker) is: run a UCC search, then send a notice of security interest to the markets where the borrower sells, and the market issues a joint check. In central-filing states (Nebraska, the Dakotas, Montana), a properly filed EFS already shifts double-pay risk to the barn, so the lender can recover from a solvent, insured counterparty. The lenders who actually lose are the ones with missing or defective filings. A Nebraska Bankers Association piece says not all lenders file EFSs and that filing errors cost them FSA protection. Those are the least likely to buy a $300-600/loan/yr monitoring tool. Price anchors are far lower: Alberta's alert service is C$52.50/yr and a Montana brand-lien filing is $25 (both from the dossier). There is also a signal-to-noise problem. October-November is when every cow-calf borrower sells calves, so 'Borrower X consigned 143 steers Thursday' is expected behavior on an operating line. The alert has value only if the lender knows which sales were authorized, which needs borrowing-base data most lenders do not hold in structured form. Expect alert fatigue within one fall run. The fraud cases in the dossier are mostly phantom collateral, forged bills of sale and inspection evasion, and the headline 2026 case was a forged bill of sale, not an exit sale; exit alerts miss all of those. Demand is also soft right now: Kansas City Fed says farm credit deterioration is easing and delinquencies are about 2% or less, so lenders are not in acute pain.

THE FIRST DOLLAR IS 9-18 MONTHS AWAY, NOT WEEK 4. The 'first 30 days' plan (a sheet and a fuzzy-match script holding lender borrower lists, then ask for $300/loan in week 4) collides with bank vendor management. The June 2023 Fed/FDIC/OCC interagency third-party risk guidance covers any business arrangement, scaled to risk. Fintech-for-banks sources describe SOC 2 Type II as close to table stakes and bank security reviews of 3-6 months. Those are consultancy and trade-press figures, not verified benchmarks, but the direction is clear. A bank compliance officer will not let a loan officer upload borrower names, family names and brands to an unvetted solo vendor's spreadsheet. The realistic 30-day outcome is one friendly loan officer informally emailing a few names, which produces anecdotes, not a priced, repeatable sale. Selling to roughly 280 agricultural banks (the dossier's estimate) one at a time, each with a long security review, makes CAC high against a Phase 1 pool of $4-13M/yr at 100% penetration. (I checked GLBA and do not count it as a killer: the privacy rule covers consumer-purpose lending, not business or agricultural loans. State confidentiality duties still need counsel.)

PHASE 3 'TITLE REGISTRY' HAS NO LEGAL HOOK, AND THE MOAT IS PUBLIC DATA. Cattle have no certificate-of-title regime. The legal notice channels are FSA direct notice and state central-filing systems, which Section 1324 of the Act lets States establish. A private registry cannot be a certified central filing system, and it does not replace the UCC-1 either (the Nebraska Bankers piece says an EFS or direct notice does not replace a UCC-1). Lenders would have to double-file and also pay the registry, so it is a convenience layer with no perfection or priority effect. Brand agencies are statutory incumbents in the proposed wedge states. In Nebraska the Brand Committee cannot record a brand transfer once a lienholder notifies it of a lien (Neb. Rev. Stat. 54-1,100), and Nebraska law already lets any bank request a state physical brand inspection at a per-head fee capped near $1.10 (LB1187 text shows the existing fee structure). The 'cornered resource' claim is weak. EFS data sits on public state master lists that registered buyers and markets receive. The private increment (d/b/a names, family names, brands) can be fed just as easily to Sale Time Systems, a cloud barn-management platform since 1988 whose listing includes lien verification and brand management, in the workflow where the consignment list already lives. Wolters Kluwer's iLien already sells generic lien monitoring to lenders and could add farm-products logic. Pre-mortem 2028: (a) barns will not share, (b) banks will not pay $300, (c) Sale Time or a Secretary of State office ships a free alert feature. None of those is fixable by founder execution alone.

objections: The 'reusable library' moat probably belongs to the OEMs, not to a two-person shop. ERCOT's own deck says the Converter Model Validation (the hardware-validation step the idea is built on) is 'generally performed in OEM's laboratory' and 'usually performed once for a certain model or family of converters'. HIL validation needs the real UPS or power-shelf controller connected to a simulator. A start-up with no purchasing leverage cannot get that hardware or firmware. ERCOT's comments say Eaton and Vertiv presented to the ERCOT Large Load Working Group on July 11 and confirmed their equipment can meet the proposed ride-through requirements. ON.energy has published NREL-lab ride-through results and claims a 500+ MW ERCOT-approved load. Crusoe is deploying 5 GW of ON.energy UPS. Once an OEM validates a family once and hands customers the PSCAD model plus a report, the independent shop is left with site-specific MQT and PSS/E paperwork. That is commodity consulting at the 30-40% margin the pitch says it will avoid. The dossier's 'highest threat' label for OEMs is correct. The dossier's two-of-three-OEMs kill trigger may already be partly tripped.

The cash timing is far worse than the pitch, and the 'why-now' is mostly stale. The compliance gate (PGRR144) is not yet law. The ERCOT page shows the Board passed it 9/15/26, status 'Pending' at the PUCT, no effective date, and no grandfathering language for Batch Zero. The 'approved' energization review only applies to Large Computational Loads (75 MW and above, 50%+ power-electronic load), and only at initial energization. Developers buy at the deadline, and energization is frozen. Abbott's Aug 3 directive means ERCOT will not authorize data centers of 75 MW and above to energize until verification is done. ERCOT expects 'several months, but less than nine months' from the Aug 20 open meeting, which could run to roughly May 2027. On Sept 21 Abbott also told TCEQ to halt all data center permits until the ERCOT audit finishes. BNEF estimates the freeze delays 49.8 GW. Batch Zero commitment deadlines (financial security, site control) are not until about June 2027. So the 'acceptance' event that triggers the 25% kicker is plausibly 9-18+ months away for most buyers. The dossier estimates 'two quarters' of slippage. The evidence supports longer. The 47 loads removed for having no dynamic model show the stick is real. They were removed on July 10 and the legacy on-ramp is closed, so that demand has already passed.

The 'acceptance expertise' moat is thin, and the market is crowded. ERCOT states that completing the MQTs 'does not constitute an endorsement' of NOGRR282 compliance. ERCOT's impact analysis budgets only 1.0 FTE (1,355 hours per year) to review model data for every Large Load. That is a few hours per project, so review will be a checklist and resubmittal loops will be short. There is little 'what ERCOT planners will accept' tacit knowledge to sell. Dynamics data is Protected Information, so precedent is invisible and cannot be marketed. ERCOT's April responses say it will not develop PSCAD models or accept field or test data in place of them, and that each Large Load Entity is responsible for its own model. ERCOT 'recommends qualified third-party support', which confirms demand but also invites many entrants. Keentel, PSC Consulting, ZEG, Powertech Labs, Electranix and Sargent & Lundy (battery sizing for ride-through) are already visible. Free ERCOT/TAMU and PNNL generic PSCAD models are accepted in the interim. The 'GAP' competitor check was wrong. Pricing power is unproven, because no transaction price for any of these services was found anywhere.

The addressable market is small and may shrink further. The CMV test and the LCL definition only bite at 75 MW and above. Sites of 25-75 MW only owe the site-specific MQT and get a community-impact data request. So the wedge is really 75-300 MW developers without in-house power staff. Batch Zero averages about 540 MW per project and 315 projects were excluded for lacking a qualifying study. Only about 7.5 GW was connected as of Dec 2025, and many queue entries are speculative or duplicated. The draft SB6 rules ($100-300k study fee and $50k per MW security) and the June 2027 commitment deadline will purge thinly capitalised developers, who are exactly this wedge. Hyperscaler tenants and big-name campuses use in-house simulators or vendor-integrated stacks (Crusoe + ON.energy). The dossier's own bottom-up pool is $10-16M one-time, and its estimate of 4-8 packages in year 1 is already well below the pitch's 12. With a 6-9 month freeze, 12 packages at $150k is not credible. A plausible realistic year 1 is a few $15-25k gap analyses and perhaps 1-3 packages.

Liability, licensing and fee-structure issues are unresolved and fall on a two-person shop. Under PGRR144 the developer attests that as-built data matches field settings. A bad model means restudy, loss of Batch Zero status or disconnection, and the developer will look to the consultant. ERCOT Dec 10 and quarterly stability assessments can revoke conditional classifications. That requires E&O cover sized for multi-hundred-MW exposure, which has not been priced. Texas engineering firms need TBPELS registration and a supervising PE, who must stand behind the seal. A 25% kicker contingent on ERCOT 'acceptance' creates an objectivity conflict for the sealing engineer. My search found no Texas rule that explicitly bans it, and the dossier flagged it as unverified, so counsel must confirm. 'Acceptance' is also not a discrete ERCOT event. The only formal gate is 'approved or additional information required' at pre-energization (LCL only), which is frozen. The kicker would be hard to define and slow to collect. OEM NDAs are the binding constraint on the reuse model and a start-up cannot force them. DCC says vendors are unfamiliar with PSCAD and treat models as proprietary IP, and that power-shelf vendors made little progress over six months. That cuts both ways. It shows the problem is real, but it also shows OEMs will not hand a third party their controllers on a fixed six-week schedule.
