result.title: Scribe Screen: Non-PHI Scribe-Cohort Run-Rate Screen for Physician Acquisitions
result.one_liner: A $4,500-7,500, five-business-day, no-PHI screen that tells a physician-practice acquirer how much of a target's trailing E/M revenue moved with ambient-scribe go-live, and hands its coding reviewer the chart-sample frame.
result.pitch:
Verdict first: the original business is dead. A privileged, coder-signed, extrapolated overpayment number at $20-45k is what both sides' lawyers avoid creating. It has no sourced buyer demand, its value was overstated roughly 3-10x, and PYA, VMG, Aprio and HIA already sell the chart audit and can add the analysis for free.

What survives is a narrower thing. Physician-practice acquirers now buy targets whose trailing twelve months contain an ambient-scribe step change. Their QoE and coding reviewers have no cheap, fast way to size how much of that is scribe-attributable before spending $15-30k on a chart audit. The Scribe Screen takes only provider-month CPT and E/M-level counts plus go-live dates, which are aggregate and non-PHI, so it can run before PHI is exchanged. In five business days it returns per-provider event-study plots, a design check that labels the result causal or descriptive depending on whether the rollout was actually staggered, a scribe-attributable EBITDA ceiling as a range, a stratified sampling frame for the buyer's chart auditor, and a seller question list. It deliberately does not estimate overpayments, so it avoids the 60-day-rule knowledge, Kovel and RWI-exclusion traps.

Sold to repeat add-on acquirers and white-labeled to second-tier coding and QoE shops, the honest ceiling is about $0.03-0.47M a year of PE buy-side revenue (central about $0.16M). That is a boutique side business for a credentialed person, not a company. There is no moat reachable within two years, and a high-school-senior founder has no credibility with this buyer set without a credentialed partner.
result.wedge_customer: Corp-dev leads or VPs of acquisitions at PE-backed physician platforms that close 4 or more add-ons a year in E/M-heavy specialties (dermatology, ophthalmology, orthopedics, GI, urology, ENT/allergy, primary care; behavioral health excluded in v1). Second channel: second-tier coding-review firms and regional QoE shops that lack data-science staff, buying it white-label or as a subcontract. PYA, VMG and Aprio are approached later, not first.
result.first_product: Scribe Screen, Stage 1 only, no PHI, 5 business days from receipt of provider-month data: (1) per-provider and per-cohort E/M-level mix aligned to go-live; (2) a design and power check that labels the output causal only when rollout staggering supports it, otherwise descriptive; (3) a scribe-attributable E/M revenue ceiling in TTM EBITDA terms as a range, stated as not an overpayment estimate; (4) a stratified sampling frame for the buyer's existing counsel-engaged chart auditor; (5) a one-page seller question list covering vendor, go-live dates, whether the tool suggests E/M levels, and time-statement settings. Chart review (Stage 2, PHI) is not built; it is a subcontract to or from an existing coding reviewer.
result.pricing: $4,500 per target under 20 providers; $7,500 for 20-150 providers (down from $20-45k, because at-risk enterprise value is about $0.2-2M rather than $8M, so the fee is 0.2-3.75% of at-risk value). Two pilots at $1,500-2,500 for a named reference, with no data-for-discount trade. Sell-side readiness and the $4-8k/month monitor are cut. Direct cost about $1-1.5k per screen, gross margin about 75-85%. About 17 screens a year reaches $100k.
result.why_now: Moderate, and weaker than the finalist file claimed. Payer downcoding is dropped as a pillar: Cigna R49 is paused, Anthem is paused, Maryland, Indiana and Illinois are restricting it, and only Centene via Cotiviti is confirmed live. What remains: (a) scribe adoption is now majority-scale (UCSF about 70% of physicians; roughly $600M of 2025 healthcare AI spend on ambient documentation), so 2026-27 targets' TTM likely contains a scribe step change; (b) the 60-day overpayment rule has been knowledge-based since 1/1/2025; (c) PE exits in 2027-29 will carry scribe-era TTM EBITDA. Headwind: PE physician-practice deals are down about 46-50% year over year.
result.moat: None of Helmer's seven Powers is reachable within two years. Scale economies and network effects do not exist at 10-30 engagements a year; switching costs are nil on a one-time project; counter-positioning is thin because incumbents lose nothing by copying; the free CMS pre-screen and cross-deal benchmark are being commoditized by Hopkins, Trilliant, Holmgren and the open Composo audit instrument. The nearest reachable power is a cornered resource: contractual rights, via an optional engagement clause, to anonymized provider-month trajectories by vendor, specialty and go-live date. That needs 30-40 engagements (2-3 years) and consent nobody has yet granted. Process power from a codified protocol with a power gate is a thin secondary. Differentiation in the meantime is operational only: fixed price, five days, no PHI, honest causal-versus-descriptive labelling.
result.bottom_up_market: Funnel reuses the dossier's PitchBook-anchored deal counts (210/300/400 PE physician-practice deals a year; the counts are sourced, the shares are my assumptions). Segment 1, targets of 20+ providers: 2/10/36 screens a year at $7,500 gives $15k/$77k/$270k. Segment 2, add-ons under 20 providers (scribe live 6+ months at LOI 15/25/35%, buyer buys a $4,500 screen 15/30/45%): 4/18/44 screens gives $18k/$79k/$198k. PE buy-side total: 6/28/80 screens, $33k/$156k/$468k a year. With non-PE acquirers at an assumed 1.5x: $50k/$234k/$700k. Central case about $0.15-0.25M a year. Sell-side and monitoring are excluded because they were cut. The original capacity of 50-100 reports a year at $30k exceeds even the high case. No sourced count exists for qualifying platforms; that is a gap.
result.competitors_and_edge: PYA, VMG, Aprio and HIA already sell buy-side coding and E/M diligence, own the buyer-counsel relationships, and can add a scribe-cohort module at near-zero marginal cost; that is the main reason this is a feature. Brellium (reported $16.7M Series A, clawback guarantee, audits scribe output) and Charta ($8.1M seed, 100% pre-bill review) are funded AI auditors, but they are post-bill and in-practice with no evidence of diligence sales, so they become post-close monitoring partners rather than rivals. Harine markets PE-facing practice analytics with the same scribe-drift story (depth unknown). Scribe vendors self-attest, and free sources (CMS, AAPC benchmarking, Hopkins, Trilliant, Holmgren, Composo) make the method copyable. The edge is operational, not structural: fixed price, five days, runs before PHI is exchanged, sold as the input to the incumbents' chart audit, and an honest power gate. The only real argument against incumbent response is that volume is too small to justify a build, which is the weakest kind of barrier.
result.riskiest_assumption: Someone with budget authority in a physician-practice acquisition will pay at least $4,500, as a separate line item, for a scribe-specific E/M run-rate screen, and the incumbent coding and QoE firms will buy or tolerate it rather than absorb it into their own scope. No buyer demand evidence exists today. The runner-up is that the staggered design supports a causal label on enough real targets, since many rollouts are group-wide.
result.two_week_test: Interview 15-20 people for under $500: 6-8 healthcare-transactions lawyers or associates, 5-7 PE VPs or corp-dev leads at platforms with add-on programs, and 4-5 current or former staff at coding-review or QoE firms (PYA, Aprio, VMG, HIA, regional CPA firms). Ask about their last three physician deals: did a scribe come up, who looked at it, what did it cost, was it a separate budget line. Then ask for commitments: would you sign a $4,500 paid pilot on your next scribe-enabled add-on, and would you white-label or subcontract this. Also ask one lawyer whether provider-month CPT counts with small-cell suppression can be shared pre-LOI without a BAA. In parallel, run a power simulation on public CMS data plus synthetic go-live schedules at 20, 40, 80 and 120 providers (group-wide, staggered, volunteer-first). Pre-registered pass: at least 6 of 15 say a scribe came up in a recent deal and someone was paid to look; at least 2 give a named, dated commitment of $4,500 or more, or at least 2 coding/QoE firms will subcontract; and the simulation supports a causal label on at least 40% of plausible rollout patterns at 40 providers. Kill if fewer than 2 commitments, if most say the QoE or coding reviewer already covers it, or if incumbents say they will build it.
result.how_critiques_were_addressed:
Critique 1 (serious, incumbents and moat). Conceded: buy-side E/M review is a served market, Brellium and Charta were missed, and no moat exists. Fixes: incumbents become the first channel (sub-vendor to second-tier coding and QoE shops), the monitor upsell is cut, and the benchmark, free pre-screen and DiD are no longer claimed as moats. Not fixed: an incumbent can still decide to build this, and the test asks them directly.

Critique 2 (fatal). Conceded as originally specified. The extrapolated overpayment number is deleted from scope, so the 60-day knowledge, RWI-exclusion and privilege-waiver problems are sidestepped rather than solved; the supported-versus-unsupported call stays with the buyer's existing counsel-engaged coding reviewer. This shrinks the product. Value was recomputed to $0.8-4M total EV and about $0.2-2M at risk for a 50-provider group, and the price fell from $20-45k to $4.5-7.5k. The data problem is addressed by a non-PHI Stage 1 on provider-month counts plus go-live dates, and audio and vendor-metadata ideas are dropped. Sell-side and monitor legs are cut, the data-for-discount pilot is dropped, and payer downcoding is removed as a why-now pillar. Not fixed: no demand evidence yet, a small and shrinking deal pool, and the seller may refuse to share go-live dates.

Critique 3 (serious). Privilege versus the number is solved by the same scoping. Timeline is now 5 days for Stage 1 only. DiD fragility is handled with a pre-sale power gate, so the output is labelled descriptive when rollout is group-wide, and output is a range and a ceiling, never a standalone escrow number. Liability is limited by no extrapolation, a cap at 1x fee and an E&O quote before the first job. Behavioral health is dropped. Not fixed: if most targets lack staggering, the product collapses into the descriptive work incumbents already do.

Founder credibility is conceded outright; it requires a credentialed partner or the idea should not be pursued. Net: the critiques are fatal to the company as pitched, and what is left is a roughly $0.15-0.25M a year boutique wedge.

result.title: Cure Desk: Cash-Worker Evidence Kit for Health Centers (post-critique)
result.one_liner: A cheap, bilingual, paper-first evidence kit and case tracker that helps Nebraska health-center CHWs document cash work for Medicaid work-requirement notices. It is a small services bolt-on, not a venture-scale company.
result.pitch: Verdict first: this is not a venture-scale software company, and I would not fund the pitch as written. The strongest honest version is a small, cheap, services-first desk for one narrow job. A Nebraska health-center CHW holds a work-requirement notice for a patient who cleans houses or does yard work for cash. The state's own declaration form (MLTC-118, which I read directly) has no employment or self-employment line and says other activities may need "a different form of verification," so that worker's route is undefined. Cure Desk fills the gap with a bilingual, paper-and-phone-first kit: a plain statement the household that paid the worker can sign (it never mentions Medicaid), a patient self-declaration worded for the state's request for "any information you have," a CHW script, and a tracker that logs what the caseworker accepted or rejected. No WhatsApp, no outbound texts to employers, no crew-leader batches, no revenue share with platforms that could replace us, no fee that rises with acceptance. We charge a flat $400 a month per health-center organization (10 cases included, $40 each after), or one statewide license to a primary care association, about 7% of the $70K staff hire it substitutes for. It works only if two things hold that nobody has shown: caseworkers treat a third-party statement as better than self-declaration for cash work, and stalled cases are proof problems rather than non-response (about 960 of roughly 1,090 Nebraska losses were non-response). At honest prices Nebraska is worth about $10-40K a year and the national figure is roughly $0.3-1.1M a year at 5-10% adoption. That is a feature or a side project, not a company. Spend two weeks on calls to test the rule signal, then stop or continue on the evidence.
result.wedge_customer: One Nebraska health-center organization with a large Spanish-speaking panel and a measurable backlog of cash-worker notices (enrollment or CHW lead as user and buyer). Reach it through the Health Center Association of Nebraska (HCAN), which aggregates the seven Nebraska FQHC organizations, so one conversation can cover all of them. Dropped: crew leaders as attesters, the refugee-language add-on (refugees and asylees lost eligibility Oct 1, 2026), and MCOs and platform partners as channels.
result.first_product:
A Cash-Work Evidence Kit, not a platform, with no custom software in v0. It has four parts:
- A bilingual one-page "statement of work performed" that a household employer can sign (dates and hours, no mention of Medicaid), handed over by the patient.
- A patient self-declaration worded for the notice's "any information you have" request.
- A CHW script.
- A spreadsheet tracker that logs the state's response and reason for every case.
The CHW keeps PHI in the health center's own systems. We hold outcome codes only. No WhatsApp and no vendor-sent texts, which removes the HIPAA BAA and TCPA problems in v0.
result.pricing: Flat subscription of $400 a month per health-center organization, with 10 cases included and $40 per case after. This is about 7% of the $70K CHW hire the buyer would otherwise make. Optional statewide license to a primary care association [assumption: $10-25K a year]. Reject credit if a state rejects for a reason our packet should have prevented. Honest caveats: 2027 allows self-declaration, so paid demand is more likely 2028+. The cheap OCR, LLM and WhatsApp cost-curve story is dropped as a why-now because it is equally available to incumbents and to health-center staff. result.moat:
None of the 7 Powers is reachable inside the 2027-28 window, and I claim no moat.
- Scale economies fail at about 10 cases a month per site.
- Switching costs are near zero because a PDF is replaceable.
- Network effects died with the batch screen.
- Counter-positioning is thin: it rests on being cheaper and less integrated than incumbents, which gets absorbed.

result.bottom_up_market:
Reachable customers times realistic annual spend, with the assumptions marked.
- National: 1,359 HRSA health-center awardees (2024, per the dossier's HRSA cite) x $4.8-8K a year (flat fee plus overage) is about $6.5-11M at full adoption. At 5-10% adoption that is about 68-136 organizations, or about $0.3-1.1M a year.

result.competitors_and_edge:
Competitors:
- Free or state-side: CMS Emmy (free, open source), state worksheets (Georgia, Ohio, Nebraska's own form), Digital Public Works, Code for America, Nava, and vendor pledges from Maximus, Optum, Gainwell and others (free through 2028).
- Approver rails: Unite Us with Fortuna (a16z Series A), Gainwell's CEV ecosystem (Argyle, Findhelp, Fortuna, Unite Us, Databricks), Helper Helper, and Findhelp with Uno Health.
- FQHC-side: Pointcare (exemption tracking only, no income packet found), CareMessage (outreach), and outsourced eligibility vendors (Optum, Panacea, Centauri).
Edge: honestly only price and format. It is the cheapest, least-integrated, paper-and-phone-first option for people with no digital trail, sold at the health-center CHW workflow level. It does not compete on state-side verification. Incumbents could extend "approver" to household employers, and any free state worksheet ends the case, so the edge is perishable.
result.riskiest_assumption: For cash-paid patients holding a Nebraska work-requirement notice, the coverage loss comes from missing or insufficient proof that a third-party statement would fix. It does not come from non-response (about 960 of roughly 1,090 Nebraska losses were non-response), and it is not already fixed by the free route (state assistance, "any information you have," or a state worksheet). If caseworkers do not treat a third-party statement as better evidence, nothing downstream matters, including attester response, willingness to pay and channel.
result.two_week_test:
Zero build, about $0 and 20-25 hours of calls and email.
- Days 1-2: write a 10-question script and a one-page bilingual statement, and write the pass and kill thresholds before any call.
- Days 1-10: speak to HCAN and the seven Nebraska FQHC enrollment or CHW leads, Legal Aid of Nebraska's help line, and DHHS or a local caseworker office. Identify yourself honestly as a researcher. Target 8 completed conversations: at least 5 CHW or enrollment staff, 1 legal aid, 2 state or caseworker.
- Core questions: of your last 20 notices touching cash or informal workers, how many were no response, responded and approved, or responded and stalled or rejected, and why? What does the state accept in place of an employment line? Has a statement from the person who paid them ever changed an outcome? How many staff hours per case? Would your finance approve $400 a month, or would you assign a CHW?
- Days 8-14: show the statement to the CHWs and any willing household-employer proxies, and count would-sign versus would-not and why.
- PASS: at least 3 of 5 or more centers report 5+ cash-worker cases in the last 60 days stalled or rejected for lack of proof, not non-response; at least one state or caseworker source says a third-party statement is better evidence or is requested in practice; at least one CHW lead says they would fund $400 a month.

result.title: Direct-Notice Desk for Cattle Lenders
result.one_liner: A fixed-fee audit, then a cheap subscription, that keeps an ag lender's Food Security Act notice on cattle collateral complete, current and provable in states with no central filing system, so the lender can force any noticed sale barn to honor its payment conditions without the barn's cooperation.
result.pitch:
Direct-Notice Desk keeps a lender's Food Security Act protection on cattle collateral complete, current and provable. This is a small niche compliance business, not the venture originally pitched; the two-sided alert network and the title registry are deleted. Under 7 U.S.C. 1631 a sale barn takes cattle free of a lender's lien unless it received written notice from the lender within the year before the sale, carrying specific content (parties, debtor identifier, counties, crop year, payment conditions), and then failed to honor those conditions. Outside the 19 states with USDA-certified central filing (Kansas is direct-notice-only; Missouri and Kentucky are absent from the USDA list), that notice is the lender's only lever. Nothing in law forces a lender to send it, courts have ruled against lenders over missing counties or identifiers, and lawyers call the fix cheap yet under-used.

We sell the credit-administration manager, not the loan officer, a $2,000 Notice Gap Audit: 10 business days, redacted spreadsheet only, a statute-checked gap report per cattle borrower, and ready-to-send notice packets mapped to the markets and buyers in each borrower's trade area. Customers who want it kept current move to $30 per borrower per year (floor $2,500) for annual re-notice, three-month amendments, receipt tracking and an examiner-ready binder.

Barns are never asked to share, pay or integrate. The statute gives the lender the lever, and a standing annual notice replaces same-day alerts. Honest size: roughly $0.2-0.9M ARR at 25-40% penetration of about 165 institutions, with a ceiling near $2M only if the program expands to all farm products. It is worth two weeks of cold outreach because the test is nearly free and the kill rule is hard: no signed paid audits, no go.
result.wedge_customer: The ag credit or loan-administration manager (owner of documentation and exams, not the relationship loan officer) at a roughly $300M-$2B community bank, or a Farm Credit association, in Kansas first, then Missouri and Kentucky, with 100+ cattle borrowers. All are outside the 19 USDA-certified central-filing states, where direct notice is the lender's only statutory protection and no free state master list, brand-lien portal or alert exists. Nebraska, Montana, the Dakotas, Oklahoma and the other certified states are excluded; Texas is excluded from the pilot because of screwworm movement controls (critic's search summary).
result.first_product: Notice Gap Audit, a 10-business-day service. Input is a redacted spreadsheet of cattle borrowers (entities, d/b/a, family names, brands, counties, last notice date). Output is a per-borrower gap report checked against 1631 (required content, one-year receipt window, three-month amendment duty, name variants, counties), a trade-area barn and buyer map built from public licensee lists, and content-checked notice packets with the debtor identifier left blank for bank staff to merge at send time, so the pilot never stores sensitive identifiers. Stage 2 is Notice Desk: annual re-notice, amendment and receipt tracking, and an examiner-ready binder, plus an optional free read-only verify page for barns. Per-consignment alerts and the registry are dropped.
result.pricing: Audit: $2,000 flat for up to 40 borrower files, credited against year one, sold as a professional-services order form. Subscription: $30 per borrower per year with a $2,500 floor per institution (about $4.5K for a 150-borrower bank); mail and filing fees at cost. The lender is the only payer; barns pay nothing. This replaces the old $300-600 per loan ask, which was 6-12x the government anchors (Alberta alert C$52.50/yr, Montana $25 per filing, North Dakota $480/yr statewide) and above the critic's $20-125 expected-loss value. remaining_holes: DEMAND EVIDENCE COMES FROM THE STATES THE REWRITE EXCLUDES. Fin-Ag v. Pipestone is South Dakota and AgCountry v. Tri-County is Minnesota. Both are central-filing (EFS) disputes. The rewrite's notice-defect story therefore rests on the wrong states and the wrong mechanism (EFS, not direct notice). Direct-notice case law does exist: State Bank of Cherry v. CGB (Ill. 2013, county omitted) and Farm Credit Midsouth v. Farm Fresh Catfish (8th Cir. 2004, strict compliance). Both are crop or catfish cases in IL and AR, and the rewrite does not cite them. The Baird Holm piece it leans on is dated July 2015 and names no cases.

THE FREE INCUMBENT SUBSTITUTE IS UNNAMED, AND LENDERS IN THE WEDGE LIKELY ALREADY DO THIS. The Kansas Bankers Association general counsel tells Kansas banks to send 'prenotification' statements to buyers the bank and borrower identify (The Kansas Banker, 2017). A TSCRA banker piece describes the same routine for Texas. The rewrite treats bankers associations and law firms only as channels, never as substitutes. The base rate of lenders doing nothing is probably lower than the pitch implies. The remaining customers are lenders with sloppy programs, and those are the least likely to buy. The rewrite restates this as 'the riskiest assumption' and defers it to the test.

PRICE STILL DOES NOT CLEAR THE LOSS MATH, AND TOTAL COST OF OWNERSHIP IS IGNORED. At the critic's community-bank rate (0.08-0.10%) on a $500K loan, all-cause expected loss is $400-500. Applying the rewrite's own 10% exit-sale share and 50% notice reach gives $20-25 per borrower per year, below the $30 fee. 'Compliance labor displaced' is never quantified. 'Mail and filing fees at cost' is also unpriced. Third-party 2026 sources put USPS Certified Mail at about $5.30, plus a $2.82-4.40 return receipt, plus postage, or roughly $7-10.50 per proven-receipt piece. At 10-15 recipient barns and buyers per borrower (my estimate), that is about $70-150 per borrower per year, 2.5-5x the subscription fee. The bank's all-in price is then well above the critic's $20-125 value ceiling.

THE TEST BAR WAS LOWERED AND DOES NOT MATCH THE SIZING. The critics' mind-changers were 5+ non-friend lenders prepaying or signing paid LOIs, plus documented cases over $250K, or each lender naming a real unauthorized exit sale with dollars. The rewrite passes on 3 order forms invoiced on delivery (not prepaid) and 3 'concrete incidents' of any size or kind, including a defective filing. It never tests the recurring $30 subscription that the market math depends on. 3 of 60 contacts is 5% conversion. Extrapolated to 165 institutions that is about 8 customers, or about $37K ARR, against a sizing that assumes 25-40% penetration. The 60 contacts may also be most of the KS/MO/KY universe (my estimate, not verified), so outreach could burn the market. The case of 10+ conversations with zero orders but 3+ incidents is neither pass nor kill.

LEGAL AND OPERATIONAL GATES ARE UNDER-SCOPED. I verified in the statute text that 7 U.S.C. 1631(f) and (g)(3) say what counts as 'receipt' is decided by the law of the state where the buyer (the barn) resides. 'Electronic delivery is arguable' from one law firm therefore settles nothing across barns in different states. The notice must also state the amount of the products and be amended within 3 months of material changes. Herd turnover makes that more data-hungry than 'annual re-notice' suggests, and the rewrite's content checklist omits 'amount'. 'Content-checked' packets leave the debtor identifier blank, so the product cannot check one of the two documented defect types (county and identifier). A 'statute-checked' verdict from a non-lawyer raises unauthorized-practice and E&O or liability-cap exposure, and only unauthorized practice is gated. The 'redacted' spreadsheet still contains borrower names, d/b/a names, family names, brands and counties, so bank confidentiality and vendor review is not avoided. 'Within an officer's signing authority' is asserted without support.

THE MOAT CLAIM IS MISLABELED. Counter-positioning against barn-paid vendors (Sale Time, ViewTrak, LMA) is irrelevant because they were never going to build a lender product. The real replicators are ag-law firms, bankers-association templates, Wolters Kluwer, and lender-side vendors such as Nortridge and Abrigo. None of them face a cannibalization conflict. BORROWER AND LOAN-OFFICER FRICTION IS UNTOUCHED. Noticed barns will issue joint-payee checks. Borrowers can move to unnoticed barns or to direct and video channels (about 31% of feeder receipts, per the critic's source). Loan officers still hold a practical veto even though the buyer is the credit-admin manager. The KBA article also flags that ACH payments cannot be made jointly, which the notice-payment-conditions design does not address. The rewrite lumps all non-adoption into 'friction' with no evidence.

SCALE: by the rewrite's own math this is a $100-400K ARR niche, not venture scale. 'Alive' holds only as a side business, and only if a young founder can sell to rural bank credit staff cold. Texas is excluded from the pilot on the strength of an unverified critic search summary.
